newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Less volatility despite data.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Less volatility despite data.

text.p: UK gilts will have little chance to wind down for Christmas this week, with a raft of key figures to wade through and U.S. authorities meeting to discuss monetary policy, analysts said.
But with a European single currency stability pact signed and settled, a U.S. rate move not expected and no key U.S. economic data due until the new year, volatility may subside.
"Now the stability pact has been signed and with no move expected from the FOMC, things could quieten down a bit," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale.
It was Fed chairman Alan Greenspan who stirred the markets into a frenzy two weeks ago by hinting that stock markets around the globe were overheated.
But the market volatility that resulted -- gilt futures have oscillated wildly in a more than three-point range so far this month -- may now die down.
On Friday, European Union leaders agreed on a stability pact to ensure members of a single currency keep their finances in order. That was seen as a large step towards the euro's birth.
And, as Rayner pointed out, none of the heavyweight U.S. figures are due until the new year.

"The current range on the spread looks solid," Rayner said. "Gilts will be fairly stable against Germany through to the new year." The gilt/Bund spread has darted up and down between 180 and 200 basis points in recent weeks. It stood at 188 basis points on Monday morning.

The UK economic data merry-go-round starts turning on Tuesday, with November's public sector borrowing requirement, followed by a "double whammy" of retail sales and labour market statistics on Wednesday and M4 money supply and building society figures on Thursday.
The week is topped off with revised Q3 GDP data on Friday.

Following October's bumper repayment of government debt, to the tune of 4.4 billion stg, the PSBR is no longer a big market worry, analysts said, even though a shortfall of 2.7 billion stg is forecast for November.
November retail sales could be more of a problem if they exceed the consensus forecast of a 0.5 percent monthly rise.
The consensus is for year-on-year growth of 3.4 percent, down from 4.1 percent in October, largely due to an exceptionally good month for retailers last November.

"The CBI (Confederation of British Industry) distributive trades and British Retail Consortium surveys both pointed to a slowdown in retail sales in November," said David Philpotts, economist at Schroders. "But this should hardly be surprising given that both are expressed relative to 12 months previously."
The basic picture remains firm, with most analysts expecting a bonanza of Christmas spending. "The evidence is that Christmas sales are strong," Rayner said.

Economists forecast a 26,000 fall in the UK jobless number in November, hinting at a further labour market tightening. But with annual average earnings growth forecast steady at 4.0 percent in October, gilt investors should not sweat too much.
Lastly, the political scene should move to the back burner this week even though John Major's Conservative government has lost its parliamentary majority.

Rayner said Monday's debate on EU fisheries policy could lead to a government defeat. "But the Ulster Unionists said they are not likely to vote against the government so they should be able to muddle on."
In terms of intra-gilt plays, analysts at Merrrill Lynch tipped index-linked gilts over their conventional counterparts.

"The recent comments by Greenspan...saw index-linked gilts lose more ground than conventional gilts," they said. "They offer good value relative to the conventional market, especially in the current fragile environment."
Don Smith, analyst at HSBC Markets, forecast continued gilt curve flattening in the months ahead as underlying inflation continues to stick close to its current 3.3 percent.
